title: Kerberos and certificates
syllabusUnit: Unit IV: Key Distribution, Kerberos & X.509 PKI
covers: Kerberos tickets, X.509, PKI & chain of trust, revocation
learningGoals: You will be able to trace the Kerberos ticket workflow (AS -> TGS -> Service).
You will be able to verify an X.509 certificate chain of trust up to a Root CA.
You will be able to compare CRLs and OCSP for certificate revocation.

lessonCards.title: The Three-Headed Dog: Kerberos
lessonCards.analogy: Buying a day-pass at the amusement park gate, then trading it for ride tickets at each roller-coaster booth.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Kerberos uses symmetric keys and tickets: 1. Authentication Server (AS) issues a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT). 2. Ticket Granting Server (TGS) trades TGT for Service Tickets. 3. Client presents Service Ticket to the file server.
lessonCards.example: User passwords never travel across the enterprise network; timestamps prevent replay attacks.

lessonCards.title: X.509 Certificates & Chain of Trust
lessonCards.analogy: A passport stamped by your state authority, which is certified by the federal embassy, which is recognized globally.
lessonCards.coreConcept: An X.509 certificate binds a domain name to a public key, signed by a Certificate Authority (CA). Browsers verify the digital signature chain up to pre-installed Root CAs.
lessonCards.example: Let's Encrypt and DigiCert act as trusted root authorities embedded inside your operating system.

lessonCards.title: Revocation: CRLs vs OCSP
lessonCards.analogy: Checking a printed list of cancelled credit cards vs calling the card hotline live at the cash register.
lessonCards.coreConcept: If a private key is compromised, the certificate must be revoked before its expiration date. Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) download bulk blacklist files. Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) queries CA status live.
lessonCards.example: OCSP Stapling lets the web server provide a time-stamped CA verification directly to connecting clients.

questions.prompt: In the Kerberos authentication protocol, what ticket does the client receive from the Authentication Server (AS)?
options: Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT)
An SSL certificate
A Google OAuth token
A Bitcoin private key
questions.explanation: The Authentication Server validates the user's password hash and returns an encrypted Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) valid for several hours.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The TGT allows the user to request individual service tickets without re-entering their password.
SSL certificates belong to PKI.
OAuth is a web authorization protocol.
Bitcoins are unrelated.
questions.realWorldExample: Microsoft Windows Active Directory domains rely on Kerberos v5 for single sign-on (SSO).

questions.prompt: Why is strict clock synchronization (usually via NTP) mandatory across all Kerberos servers and clients?
options: Kerberos tickets contain timestamps to prevent replay attacks; clock skew exceeding 5 minutes causes authentication failure
To make screensavers sync up
Because CPU transistors only count seconds
To ensure backup tapes run at midnight
questions.explanation: Kerberos uses timestamps in authenticators to defeat replay attacks without storing past message caches; clocks must stay within 5 minutes.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Timestamps expire quickly to invalidate intercepted authentication packets.
Screensavers have no security role.
Silicon clocks measure arbitrary cycles.
Backup scheduling is separate.
questions.realWorldExample: If a workstation clock drifts by more than 5 minutes from the Domain Controller, login fails with KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW.

questions.prompt: In an X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), how does your browser verify that 'https://google.com' is authentic?
options: It follows digital signatures up the chain of trust until reaching a trusted Root CA pre-installed in the OS
It pings the website's IP address
It checks if the website has a green logo
It sends an email to the webmaster
questions.explanation: The server certificate is signed by an Intermediate CA, which is signed by a Root CA. The browser verifies each signature mathematically using the signer's public key.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The cryptographic signature chain of trust anchors into local root trust stores.
Ping only verifies network routing.
Logos are easily cloned by phishing sites.
Email verification is manual and unauthenticated.
questions.realWorldExample: Operating systems maintain trusted Root CA stores (e.g. Mozilla, Apple, Microsoft root stores).

questions.prompt: What critical information is contained inside an X.509 digital certificate?
options: Subject domain name, Subject public key, Issuer CA, Validity dates, and Issuer's digital signature
The user's credit card number
The server's root password
The source code of the website
questions.explanation: RFC 5280 defines X.509 v3 fields: Subject identity, Public key, Issuer identity, Serial number, Validity period, and CA cryptographic signature.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Identity bound to public key, verified by CA signature.
Certificates never contain private financial data.
Private passwords must NEVER appear in public certificates.
Source code is hosted on servers.
questions.realWorldExample: Inspect any padlock icon in your browser to view the X.509 certificate fields and issuer chain.

questions.prompt: What is the primary advantage of Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) over Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs)?
options: OCSP queries real-time status of a single certificate without downloading massive multi-megabyte revocation lists
OCSP encrypts all network cables
OCSP eliminates the need for Certificate Authorities
OCSP makes web servers 100% immune to malware
questions.explanation: CRLs grow continually larger, wasting bandwidth and mobile data; OCSP allows checking a single certificate's status on demand in milliseconds.
wrongExplanations: Correct! OCSP provides lightweight, real-time revocation status checks.
OCSP does not encrypt physical cables.
OCSP responders are operated by Certificate Authorities.
Revocation checking does not prevent web server malware.
questions.realWorldExample: OCSP Stapling (RFC 6066) speeds up TLS handshakes by attaching the signed OCSP response directly to the server certificate.

questions.prompt: What happens if a Certificate Authority's master private key is stolen by a malicious adversary?
options: The attacker can forge valid certificates for any domain on earth and execute undetectable Man-in-the-Middle attacks
Nothing happens because certificates are free
All web browsers turn red
Internet cables automatically shut down
questions.explanation: A compromised Root CA allows adversaries to generate counterfeit certificates for google.com or bank domains that all browsers accept as genuine.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Root CA compromise shatters the foundation of web PKI trust.
Financial cost is irrelevant to cryptographic trust.
Browsers accept validly signed fake certs without warning.
Network hardware cannot discern key theft.
questions.realWorldExample: In 2011, Dutch CA DigiNotar was hacked and issued 500+ fraudulent certificates, resulting in the entire CA being distrusted and declared bankrupt.

ashRecap: Kerberos gives you trusted day-passes across the office network. X.509 certificates give websites trusted digital passports signed by Root Authorities!
